ov: Three living species of humped desert animals: the one-humped dromedary (94% of the world’s camels), the two-humped Bactrian camel, and the endangered wild Bactrian camel. The humps store fat, not water.

why.dm: Dromedaries and Bactrian camels are domestic, but the wild Bactrian camel is a separate species, with only about 1,000 left.
why.dg: Its sheer size means it can hurt people, though with proper handling that is unlikely.

rg: Mostly domestic. The dromedary comes from the hot deserts of the Arabian Peninsula and the Sahara; the Bactrian camel from the steppes of Central Asia.
df: Desert plants. A thick, leathery lining to the mouth lets camels chew thorny ones.

cf.tip: A llama is a South American relative of the camel but not a true camel, and it has no hump.

fx: A dromedary can go as long as 10 days between drinks, even in very hot weather.
notes: Group entry for the genus; grp links the dromedary page (there’s no Bactrian page). The cf "no hump" is general knowledge; Wikipedia’s Camel article only says llamas are not true camels.
